prompt.context: Our client is a start-up with the ability to deliver broadband (high-speed) internet to commercial airlines. They would charge customers on a per-flight pricing model and would have to invest relatively little up front, keeping most of the revenues. There is general interest in broadband internet from the airline industry.
prompt.question: How would you help them think about their offering? Specifically: (1) Estimate the market size for broadband for airlines. (2) Assess whether the client can break even. (3) What other factors should the client consider before entering this market?

clarifying_info.q: How does the client plan to charge customers?
clarifying_info.a: On a per-flight (per leg) pricing model.
The company holds the patent on the high-speed connection. There are low-speed internet connections that could be considered competition.

clarifying_info.q: How many planes are in scope?

clarifying_info.a: Relatively little upfront investment; the start-up would keep most of the revenues.

exhibits.title: Seat and Traveler Data by Class
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down seats per plane, load factor, and share of business travelers for First Class and Coach, used to estimate the number of laptop users per plane.
exhibits.data: First Class: 20 seats, 0.75 load factor, 100% business travelers. Coach: 180 seats, 0.75 load factor, 30% business travelers.

exhibits.title: Price vs. Penetration Rate
exhibits.shows: A chart or table showing the number of users and resulting revenue per flight at various price points ($5, $10, $15, $20, $25) assuming 100 passengers, used to identify the optimal price.

framework: Market sizing: estimate total addressable market (number of planes, flights per year, laptop users per flight, willingness to pay)
Revenue model: price per user per leg, penetration rate, revenue per plane per year
Break-even analysis: determine revenue needed per plane to be profitable; back into required users per leg
Competitive landscape: existing or potential low-speed internet alternatives; patent protection
Risks: technology reliability, airline partnership terms, customer adoption, regulation
Go/no-go recommendation: synthesize findings into a clear market-entry decision

questions.prompt: Estimate the market size for broadband for airlines. (Present Exhibit 1; 3,000 planes are in scope.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through a structured build-up: seats by class → apply load factor → apply % business travelers (proxy for laptop users) → sum across classes → scale by 90% laptop ownership assumption → multiply by planes and legs per year. Strong candidates will arrive at ~300 million potential user-legs per year.

math.setup: Use Exhibit 1 data. First Class: 20 seats × 0.75 load = 15 filled × 100% biz = 15 biz travelers. Coach: 180 seats × 0.75 load = 135 filled × 30% biz = 40.5 biz travelers. Total = 55.5 laptop users/plane × 90% laptop ownership ≈ 50 laptop users/plane. Scale: 3,000 planes × 2,000 legs/plane × 50 laptop users/plane.
math.answer: Approximately 300 million potential user-legs per year.

questions.prompt: Conduct a break-even analysis. The company needs $250,000 per plane per year in revenue to be profitable. What price should they charge, and will they break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert the annual revenue target to a per-leg figure, then use Exhibit 2 to find the price that generates enough users per leg. The optimal price from Exhibit 2 is $15 (highest revenue per flight = $300). At $15 and 50 laptop users/leg, penetration rate is ~20%, yielding ~10 users/leg. This exceeds the 8 users/leg needed to break even.

math.setup: Annual revenue target = $250,000/plane. Legs per plane per year = 2,000. Optimal price from Exhibit 2 = $15 (maximizes revenue at $300/flight per 100 passengers). Required users/leg at $15 to break even: $125/leg ÷ $15/user. Actual estimated users/leg: 50 laptop users × 20% penetration.
steps: Users needed per leg at $15: $125 / $15 ≈ 8 users/leg
Exhibit 2 revenue check: at $15, 20 users per 100 passengers → $300/flight (highest revenue point)
Estimated actual users at $15: 50 laptop users/leg × 20% penetration = 10 users/leg
10 users/leg > 8 users/leg required → break-even is achievable
math.answer: Yes, the client should break even. At $15/user and ~10 users per leg, they exceed the 8 users/leg threshold needed to cover the $250K/plane annual target.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should the start-up consider before entering this market?

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Existing low-speed internet providers on flights
Potential entrants once market is proven
Intellectual property: client holds patent on high-speed connection — strong moat
Telecom giants that may enter with scale advantages

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Airlines unwilling to share cabin infrastructure
Revenue share terms negotiated by airlines eroding margins
Cybersecurity risks of open in-flight WiFi

categories.name: Demand & Pricing
ideas: Price elasticity beyond the modeled range
Business vs. leisure traveler mix variation by route
Future pricing pressure as competition grows

recommendation: Enter the market: the broadband-for-airlines opportunity is large (~300M user-legs/year) and the economics are viable — at $15/user, the client exceeds the break-even threshold of 8 users/leg with an estimated 10 users/leg.
The patent on high-speed connectivity provides a defensible competitive moat in the near term.
Prioritize airlines and routes with high business-traveler mix to maximize penetration and revenue per plane.
risks: Regulatory hurdles (FAA approval) could delay rollout
Low-speed competitors may undercut on price even without matching quality
Airlines may negotiate revenue-share terms that compress margins
next_steps: Secure formal airline partnerships and negotiate favorable revenue-share agreements
Pursue FAA certification and technical validation for the high-speed system
Pilot on a subset of planes to validate adoption and refine pricing assumptions
